newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israelis on guard against more suicide attacks.
newsitem.headline: Israelis on guard against more suicide attacks.

text.p: Israel girded for more suicide attacks on Sunday with a top security official citing information that Islamic militants might strike again after last week's bloody Jerusalem bombing.
Thousands of policemen guarded shopping malls, bus stations and other places where crowds gather in Israel's main cities and stopped cars for inspection along key roads.

Troops overnight arrested another 37 Palestinians in the West Bank suspected of involvement in Islamic militant groups, bringing to 116 the number rounded up since two bombers killed 13 people in an Israeli market last Wednesday.

Police chief Assaf Hefetz, asked if Israel had specific information about more attacks, told army radio: "It's more than just an estimate. We have a series of...details that point to this possibility."
He said after four days of investigation officials were still uncertain who carried out the attack. "In my opinion, we still don't have a lead."
A leaflet issued in the name of the Islamic militant Hamas group claimed responsibility and gave Israel until 9 p.m. (1800 GMT) on Sunday to release Palestinian prisoners.
The leaflet did not say what would happen if Israel refused, and Israeli and Palestinian officials have both cast doubt on the authenticity of the claim.
The suicide bombing revived haunting memories of a bombing spree last year in which Islamic miliants struck four times in nine days, killing 57 people.

Para-military border policeman armed with automatic rifles patrolled a stretch of Jerusalem road from the bombing site at the Mahane Yehuda market to the city's central station where morning commuters rushed to catch their buses.
"I'm not afraid. There's a God in heaven...It's all in God's hands," said Jerusalem-born Moshe Levy, 74, boarding a bus for a day of recreation in Tel Aviv.
Two of the four bombs last year exploded on Jerusalem buses.
"Coming to Israel you make a decision to put yourself in a place where things happen," said tourist Miriam Ratowitz, 22, of Chicago, who was waiting for a bus with American friends.
Police later held up traffic for nearly an hour near the station while sappers exploded a duffel bag left behind by a traveller and suspected to have contained a bomb.

Israel suspended already dormant peace talks with the Palestinians as a result of the bombing and sealed off the West Bank and Gaza Strip, barring tens of thousands of Palestinians from reaching their jobs in the Jewish state.

Palestinian President Yasser Arafat accused Israel of imposing collective punishment on Palestinians and expressed hope U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross, due later this week on another mediation mission, could put peacemaking back on track.
"I hope that he can push again the peace process for the accurate and honest implementation of what has been signed," Arafat told reporters in Gaza.
Top Israeli security officials met their Palestinian counterparts overnight to discuss the investigation into Wednesday's bombing, security sources said.
Netanyahu has accused Arafat of doing "damn all" to stamp out Palestinian violence and of creating an atmposphere in which Islamic militants feel free to launch attacks against Israel.
Israel and the PLO are partners in peace deals aimed at giving Palestinians self-rule in the West Bank and Gaza Strip and Israelis security through cooperation with PLO police.
Palestinians have conditioned a resumption of security cooperation with the Jewish state on a halt in Israeli settlement activity in the West Bank.
